passage:
Subject: Still here, still queuing

Hi Aditi,

Four visits to the tehsil office now. Each time a different missing form. Yesterday my token number was 212, and I honestly felt like a number instead of a person 😅 I nearly told myself nothing ever works here and stopped trying.

But that thinking only lets the system off the hook. So I wrote the whole process, forms, counters, timings, on one page and dropped it in our neighbourhood group. Two neighbours used it and finished in one visit each. I am also going to sign the petition for an online tracking system.

Come with me on Sunday to the citizens' meeting? I'd like company, and you're good with paperwork.

Zainab

qa.q: How many visits has Zainab made to the tehsil office?
How does Zainab feel about the delays, and what shows it?
qa.a: Zainab feels worn down and like "a number instead of a person", and was tempted to think nothing ever works, but chooses not to let cynicism win.

qa.q: What else could Zainab do to keep engaging with the problem?
qa.a: Keep the one-page guide updated, help more neighbours through the process, and back the petition for online tracking.

qa.q: How might the two neighbours have seen Zainab's one-page guide?
qa.a: As real help, since each of them finished in one visit instead of returning again and again.

grounding: Repeated delays leave Zainab feeling like a number, but Zainab chooses engagement by writing a guide for others and supporting reform.

passage:
By the third month of trying to transfer his late father's scooter to his name, Samir had stopped expecting anything from the transport office in Indore. Every visit ended the same way: a new form, a shrug. "We're just numbers to them," he told his friend Sahil over chai.
Sahil nodded. "Everyone says that. Then they pay an agent."
Samir almost agreed. He was so tired. But he thought of his mother, who had asked him to handle it so she wouldn't have to stand in those lines.
So he did something different. He downloaded the department's citizen charter, which listed every document and timeline. He printed it and went back. When the clerk asked for yet another form, he politely pointed to the charter. The transfer was done in two weeks.
Afterwards, Samir wrote a one-page guide in simple Hindi and pinned it on the notice board of his building. Three neighbours used it that month.

qa.q: What did Samir download from the department?
qa.a: The citizen charter, which listed every document and timeline.

qa.q: What was Samir feeling by the third month?
qa.a: He felt tired and disillusioned, believing people were just numbers to the transport office.

qa.q: How did Samir choose engagement over cynicism?
qa.a: He learned the official procedure through the citizen charter, used it politely at the counter, and wrote a simple guide to help his neighbours.

qa.q: How might Sahil see Samir's success?
qa.a: Sahil may feel surprised and perhaps inspired, having assumed an agent was the only way.

grounding: Repeated delays make the protagonist feel like a number, but he chooses engagement: learning procedures and helping others navigate them.

passage:
"Parul, I give up. Six months for a simple address change on my voter ID. Six!"
"You look exhausted, Bidisha."
"I am. They lose the file, they ask for the same paper, they don't answer the phone. What's the point of any of it?"
"I felt like that about my ration card last year."
"And?"
"And then I realised the people who give up are exactly who the system forgets. So I learned the online tracking system and filed an appeal."
Bidisha rubbed her eyes. "I don't have the energy to become an expert."
"You don't have to be. Sit with me on Saturday. I'll show you the portal. And there's a residents' group that's pushing the office to publish file timelines. They need people who've actually had bad experiences."
"You think it'll change anything?"
"Slowly. But complaining in our kitchen changes nothing."
Bidisha laughed tiredly. "Saturday, then. Bring snacks."

qa.q: How long had Bidisha waited for the address change on the voter ID?
What was Bidisha feeling when she said "What's the point of any of it?"
qa.a: She felt exhausted and disillusioned, ready to give up on the system.

qa.q: What did Parul suggest instead of cynicism?
qa.a: Learning the online tracking system together, filing an appeal if needed, and joining a residents' group pushing for published file timelines.

qa.q: How might Parul see Bidisha's frustration?
qa.a: Parul recognises it from the ration-card struggle last year and wants to help Bidisha turn tiredness into engagement.

grounding: Repeated delays make the protagonist feel like a number; a friend helps her choose engagement by learning procedures and supporting reform.
